sub: Named after “the pen” (al-qalam) in ayah 1; also called Nūn
theme: Allah defends the Prophet ﷺ against the charge of madness and praises his character. He exposes a leading opponent, warns Makkah through the owners of a garden, and tells the Prophet ﷺ to be patient.
story: One of the earliest surahs revealed in Makkah, sent when opposition to the Prophet ﷺ had turned harsh. The disbelievers called him majnūn, mad, saying: “You to whom the Reminder is sent down, you are mad” (15:6).

The surah answers them: his message and his conduct prove his sanity. It tells him not to compromise, exposes a leading opponent, and warns Makkah with the story of the garden. Much of it is reported to concern al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah and Abū Jahl.
It closes by telling the Prophet ﷺ to endure patiently, unlike Yūnus when he left his people, and answers the charge of madness again: this is only a reminder to the worlds.

sections.title: By the pen: you are not mad
sections.meaning: Allah swears by the pen and what is written: by your Lord’s favour, you are not mad. You have a reward that never ends and a great character. Soon you and they will see which side is truly afflicted, and your Lord knows best who strayed and who is guided.
points: Nūn; an oath by the pen and what they write
Not mad, by Allah’s favour; a reward never cut off
You are upon a great character
You’ll see who is afflicted; Allah knows who is guided
sections.matters: It is a defence of the Prophet ﷺ sworn by Allah Himself. The accusation of madness is answered with his character, the clearest proof of his truth, and a promise that time will show who was lost.
sections.story: The idolaters called the Prophet ﷺ possessed and mad: “You to whom the Reminder is sent down, you are mad” (15:6). Allah revealed ayah 2 to reject their claim.
explained: Nūn is one of the separate letters that open some surahs; Allah knows its meaning. He swears by the pen, either the pens people write knowledge with or the Pen that wrote all of destiny, and by what is written. The point sworn to: by your Lord’s favour, you are not mad.

A madman’s work bears no fruit, but his reward never ends. His character is ʿaẓīm: asked about it, ʿĀʾishah said his character was the Qurʾan. He never struck a servant and never took revenge for himself. Soon both sides will see who is truly maftūn, and Allah knows who is guided.
teaches: Knowledge and writing are blessings worth an oath.
Good character is a powerful proof of truth.
Let insults pass; time and Allah will judge.
The Prophet ﷺ is our model of character.
sections.hook: It opens with the letter Nūn and the pen. The word “mad” (majnūn) from ayah 2 returns in ayah 51, just before the surah ends.

sections.title: Don’t give in to the deniers
sections.meaning: Don’t obey the deniers: they want you to soften so they can soften. And don’t obey the constant swearer, slanderer and tale-carrier, who blocks good, is cruel and notorious, and calls Allah’s ayat old legends because he has wealth and sons. He will be branded on the nose.
points: Don’t obey the deniers; they want you to compromise
Don’t obey the oath-swearer, the slanderer, the tale-carrier
Blocks good, transgresses, sins; cruel and notorious
Wealth and sons make him call the ayat old legends
We will brand him on the snout
sections.matters: It draws a line: the truth is not traded for a truce. The list of vices shows what kind of people led the opposition, set against the great character praised just before.
sections.story: Makkah’s leaders asked the Prophet ﷺ to stay quiet about their gods so they would leave him alone. The man described is reportedly al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah; other reports name al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq or al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth.
explained: The deniers hoped for a deal: stay silent about their idols, and they would ease off. Allah forbids it; the Prophet ﷺ must not yield. Then comes a portrait of a leading opponent. He swears constantly because he is a liar, mocks people, and carries tales to set them against each other.

He withholds good and keeps others from Islam, oversteps limits, and piles up sins. He is harsh and cruel, and zanīm, marked out by his evil. Because he has wealth and sons, he calls the Qurʾan “legends of the ancients”. Allah will brand him on the nose, a disgrace that won’t fade.
teaches: Never compromise on the truth to please people.
Swearing all the time is a sign of lying.
Backbiting and spreading tales are grave sins.
Wealth and children can breed arrogance instead of gratitude.
sections.hook: “Do not obey” opens ayah 8 and again ayah 10. Nine faults then follow in a row, from ḥallāf (10) to zanīm (13). Page 564 ends at ayah 16.

sections.title: The owners of the ruined garden
sections.meaning: Makkah is tested like the owners of a garden, who swore to harvest at dawn, without saying in shāʾ Allāh, and keep the poor out. Overnight the garden was destroyed. Seeing it, they blamed each other, admitted their wrong and turned to their Lord. Such is worldly punishment; the Hereafter’s is greater.
points: They swore to harvest at dawn, without saying in shāʾ Allāh
A calamity struck at night; the garden turned black
Whispering at dawn: no poor person gets in today
“We are lost!” No: “we are deprived”
The best of them: why didn’t you glorify Allah?
Blame, confession, and hope for something better
Such is the punishment; the Hereafter’s is greater
sections.matters: It is a mirror for Makkah, blessed with wealth and with a Prophet ﷺ, yet rejecting both. Blessings kept from the poor and credited to one’s own power can vanish overnight.
sections.story: Reportedly a garden near Ṣanʿāʾ in Yemen, though one report places it in Ethiopia. A righteous father left a share of every harvest for the poor. His sons inherited it and decided the family needed it all.
explained: Allah tested Makkah, with blessings or, in one view, with famine, as He tested the garden’s owners. They swore to cut the fruit at first light, before the poor arrived, without saying in shāʾ Allāh. While they slept, a calamity, reportedly fire, swept the garden and left it black as night.

At dawn they called each other and set out whispering: no poor person gets in today. Sure of their power, they arrived to find ruin. First they thought they were lost, then realised: we are deprived. The best of them said: didn’t I tell you to glorify Allah?

They glorified their Lord and admitted their wrong, blamed each other, then confessed together and hoped for a better garden. Reportedly they repented sincerely and were given one. Such is punishment in this world, and the Hereafter’s is far greater.
teaches: Say in shāʾ Allāh when planning; don’t rely on your own power.
Giving the poor their share brings blessing; withholding it brings loss.
Blaming each other doesn’t fix a shared mistake; repentance does.
Warning others isn’t enough if you then follow them into wrong.
sections.hook: The story starts at the top of page 565 (ayah 17). Their words change step by step: “we are lost” (26), “we are deprived” (27), “we were wrongdoers” (29), “we were transgressors” (31).

sections.title: The obedient and the criminals aren’t equal
sections.meaning: The God-conscious have Gardens of Delight with their Lord. Will Allah treat Muslims like criminals? How can you judge like that? Do you have a scripture promising you whatever you like, or a binding oath from Allah? Who guarantees it? Bring your partners, if you are truthful.
points: Gardens of Delight for the God-conscious
Muslims like criminals? How do you judge?
A scripture promising you whatever you choose?
A binding oath from Us? Who guarantees it?
Or partners? Then bring them
sections.matters: It exposes wishful thinking. Justice demands that the obedient and the guilty are not treated alike, and the deniers have no book, promise or backer for their claim to a better Hereafter.
sections.story: The Makkan disbelievers said: “If we are raised again, we will be given better than you.” Ayah 35 was revealed to reject this.
explained: After the ruined garden comes the other garden: jannāt an-naʿīm, kept with their Lord for the muttaqīn. The deniers claimed they would get more than the believers in the Hereafter. Allah asks: would He treat those who submit like criminals? In this world wrongdoers often escape, so a Day of justice must come.

Then a chain of challenges. Do you have a revealed book you read that promises you whatever you pick? Do you hold oaths from Allah, binding until the Resurrection? Ask them which of them will guarantee that. Or do they have partners to back it? Let them bring them. They have none of these.
teaches: Hope needs a real basis, not wishful thinking.
Allah’s justice will separate the obedient from the guilty.
Taqwā is the path to the Gardens of Delight.
sections.hook: It opens the second ruku at 34. A chain of “or” (am) questions follows: a scripture (37), oaths (39), partners (41). Ayah 40 breaks the chain with “Ask them”.

sections.title: The Day they cannot prostrate
sections.meaning: On the Day the shin is uncovered, the deniers are called to prostrate but cannot, eyes lowered in disgrace, because they refused while healthy. Leave them to Allah: He leads them on step by step and gives them time. They owe the Prophet ﷺ no fee, and they don’t hold the unseen.
points: The shin uncovered; called to prostrate, they cannot
Eyes lowered: they refused when they were healthy
Leave them to Me; I lead them on and give respite
Do you charge a fee? Do they hold the unseen?
sections.matters: Refusing to bow to Allah now brings the inability to bow later. It also warns that ease and delay can be a trap, and reminds that the Prophet ﷺ asked nothing of them.
sections.story: No specific incident. It continues the warning to Makkah’s deniers and comforts the Prophet ﷺ, who is told to leave their punishment to Allah.
explained: Yawma yukshafu ʿan sāq: either an idiom for the most terrible hour, as the Arabs said war “bared its shin”, or, as an authentic hadith describes, Allah uncovers His Shin, unlike anything created. Believers fall in prostration. Those who prostrated for show try, but their backs become one rigid plate.

Eyes lowered, covered in humiliation, they had been called to prostrate while healthy and refused. So leave the deniers of the Qurʾan to Allah. He draws them on gradually with blessings they mistake for honour, then seizes them; His plan is firm. They owe no fee, and have no knowledge of the unseen.
teaches: Bow to Allah now, while you still can.
Prostration done for show fails on that Day.
Blessings given to wrongdoers can be a trap.
Leave the outcome of stubborn opponents to Allah.
sections.hook: “Prostration” (as-sujūd) comes in both 42 and 43. Page 566 starts at ayah 43. The “or” (am) questions return in 46–47, and yaktubūn (47) echoes yasṭurūn in ayah 1.

sections.title: Patience, unlike the man of the fish
sections.meaning: Be patient with your Lord’s decision, unlike Yūnus, who cried out from inside the fish in distress. Without his Lord’s favour he would have been cast on bare land, blamed, but his Lord chose him. The disbelievers nearly topple you with their stares and call you mad, yet the Qurʾan is a reminder for all.
points: Be patient; don’t be like the man of the fish
A favour saved him; his Lord chose him
Their looks almost make you slip; they say he is mad
It is only a reminder to the worlds
sections.matters: It ends with the key instruction: be patient with people while awaiting Allah’s decision. Yūnus’s story shows the cost of haste and the mercy that follows repentance. The last ayah answers the charge of madness once more.
sections.story: Reportedly the disbelievers asked a man known for the evil eye to strike the Prophet ﷺ with it. Allah protected him and revealed ayah 51. Another view: it describes their glaring hatred.
explained: Be patient with what your Lord decrees and commands. Don’t be like ṣāḥib al-ḥūt, Yūnus, who left his people in anger before Allah’s permission. Swallowed by a fish, he called out from the darkness, full of grief: lā ilāha illā anta subḥānaka innī kuntu min aẓ-ẓālimīn.

Had his Lord’s favour not reached him by accepting his repentance, he would have been thrown onto bare land in disgrace. Instead his Lord chose him and made him righteous. The disbelievers, hearing the Qurʾan, glare at you so hard they almost knock you down, and call you mad. Yet it is only a reminder for the worlds.
teaches: Patience with people is part of calling them to Allah.
Don’t give up on people in anger or haste.
Sincere repentance turns disgrace into honour.
Seek Allah’s protection from the evil eye and envy.
sections.hook: The surah ends where it began: “he is mad” (51) answers “you are not mad” (2). Yūnus is not named; he is called “the companion of the fish” (48).

groups.text: By the pen and what they write: by your Lord’s favour, you are not mad.
You have a reward that never ends, and you are upon a great character.
Soon all will see who is truly afflicted. Allah knows best who strayed and who is guided.
Don’t obey the deniers. They want you to soften your stand so they will soften theirs.
Don’t obey the swearer, slanderer, tale-carrier, blocker of good, sinner, and the cruel, notorious man.
Because of wealth and sons he calls Our ayat old legends. We will brand him on the snout.
Makkah is tested like the garden’s owners, who swore to harvest at dawn without saying in shāʾ Allāh.
A calamity from Allah struck the garden at night, leaving it black and stripped.
At dawn they set off whispering, determined to keep every poor person out.
Seeing it ruined, they thought they were lost, then knew they were deprived. The best of them rebuked them.
They glorified Allah, admitted their wrong, blamed each other, confessed and hoped for something better.
Such is punishment in this world; the Hereafter’s is greater, if they only knew.
The God-conscious have Gardens of Delight. Would Allah treat Muslims like criminals? How do you judge?
Do you have a scripture that promises you whatever you choose?
Or binding oaths from Allah? Who guarantees it? Or partners? Bring them, if truthful.
On the Day the shin is bared, they can’t prostrate, eyes lowered in disgrace; they refused while healthy.
Leave the deniers to Allah: He draws them on unaware and gives them time. His plan is firm.
Are they burdened by a fee you charge? Or do they hold the unseen and write it down?
Be patient for your Lord’s decision; don’t be like Yūnus, who cried out in distress.
Allah’s favour saved him from being cast off in blame. His Lord chose him and made him righteous.
Disbelievers almost topple you with their looks, calling you mad. The Qurʾan is only a reminder to the worlds.

1.explain: Nūn: a separate letter whose meaning Allah knows. Al-qalam: the pen people write with, or the Pen that wrote destiny. Mā yasṭurūn: what they write, or what the angels record.

2.explain: Bi-niʿmati rabbik: by your Lord’s favour of prophethood and a sound mind, you are not majnūn. It rejects their charge of madness.
2.why: The idolaters said: “You to whom the Reminder is sent down, you are mad” (15:6), claiming a devil possessed him. Allah revealed this ayah to deny it.

3.explain: Ajran ghayra mamnūn: a reward that is never cut off or reduced, for conveying the message and bearing their abuse patiently.

4.explain: Khuluq ʿaẓīm: a great character, or a great religion, Islam. His character was the Qurʾan: he did what it commanded and avoided what it forbade, with modesty, kindness, bravery and forgiveness.

5.explain: Fa-satubṣiru wa yubṣirūn: you will see and they will see, whether in this life or on the Day of Judgement.

6.explain: Al-maftūn: the one afflicted with madness, lured away from the truth. Time will show it was not him but his accusers.

7.explain: Allah knows who has strayed from His path and who is guided. It is a threat to the misguided and a promise to the guided.

8.explain: Al-mukadhdhibīn: those who deny you and the truth. Obeying them only leads to harm, since they call only to their own desires.
8.why: Revealed about the idolaters of Quraysh, who called the Prophet ﷺ to his forefathers’ religion and asked him to hold back from them so they would hold back from him.

9.explain: Tudhinu: soften, meet them halfway, such as by staying silent about their gods, so they would ease off. Bending the religion like this is not allowed.

10.explain: Ḥallāf: one who swears a lot, and constant swearing goes with lying. Mahīn: contemptible and low-minded, with no aim beyond his own desires.
10.why: Reportedly revealed about al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah. Other reports name al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth or al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq. The description still applies to anyone like him.

11.explain: Hammāz: a fault-finder who mocks and backbites. Mashshāʾ bi-namīm: goes around carrying tales to turn people against each other. The Prophet ﷺ said the tale-carrier will not enter Paradise.

12.explain: Mannāʿ lil-khayr: withholds good, from what he owes others to letting his family near Islam. Muʿtadin: oversteps limits against people. Athīm: steeped in sin.

13.explain: ʿUtull: harsh, rough and greedy. Baʿda dhālik: on top of all that. Zanīm: either someone attached to a tribe he doesn’t truly belong to, or someone marked by his evil, like a sheep with a notched ear.

14.explain: An kāna dhā mālin wa banīn: because he has wealth and sons. His blessings made him arrogant instead of grateful.

15.explain: When the Qurʾan is recited to him, he calls it asāṭīr al-awwalīn: legends of earlier peoples. That is how he repays Allah’s favours.

16.explain: Sa-nasimuhu ʿalal-khurṭūm: We will brand him on the snout. Either a mark on his face in the Hereafter, or a disgrace that never leaves him. Reportedly the man was struck on the nose by a sword at Badr.

17.explain: Balawnāhum: We tested Makkah, with blessings such as wealth and the Prophet ﷺ, or with famine. Aṣḥāb al-jannah: garden owners who swore to cut the fruit muṣbiḥīn, at first light, before the poor came.

18.explain: Wa lā yastathnūn: they didn’t add “in shāʾ Allāh”. Another view: they made no exception for the poor, meaning to keep everything.

19.explain: Ṭāʾif: a calamity from your Lord that came by night, reportedly a fire, while they were asleep and unaware.

20.explain: Kaṣ-ṣarīm: like a harvested field stripped bare, or black like the darkest night, burnt to ash.

21.explain: At dawn they called one another awake, still unaware of what had happened in the night.

22.explain: Ughdū: set out early to your ḥarth, your crops and fruit, if you mean to harvest.

23.explain: Yatakhāfatūn: whispering to each other, so no one would overhear and tell the poor.

24.explain: Their whispered plan: not a single miskīn, poor person, gets into the garden today.

25.explain: ʿAlā ḥard: set on withholding, or with firm resolve, or angry at the poor. Qādirīn: sure they had full control over it.

26.explain: Innā la-ḍāllūn: we have lost our way; this can’t be our garden.

27.explain: Bal naḥnu maḥrūmūn: no, it is ours, and we have been deprived of its fruit, because we meant to deprive the poor.

28.explain: Awsaṭuhum: the most just and best of them. Law lā tusabbiḥūn: why don’t you glorify Allah, by saying in shāʾ Allāh or by thanking Him? He had warned them, yet went along.

29.explain: Subḥāna rabbinā: they declared their Lord free of any injustice and admitted they were ẓālimīn, wrongdoers, for denying the poor.

30.explain: Yatalāwamūn: they turned on each other, each blaming the others, though they had done it together.

31.explain: Yā waylanā: woe to us. Ṭāghīn: we all overstepped the limits, in Allah’s right and in the right of the poor.

32.explain: They hope their Lord will replace it with better, in this life or as reward in the Hereafter. Rāghibūn: turning to Him in hope. Reportedly they repented sincerely and received a better garden.

33.explain: Kadhālika al-ʿadhāb: this is how worldly punishment comes to those who defy Allah and withhold the poor’s right. The Hereafter’s punishment is greater.

34.explain: Al-muttaqīn: those who guard themselves against disbelief and sin. With their Lord are jannāt an-naʿīm: gardens of lasting delight.

35.explain: Al-muslimīn: those who submit and obey. Al-mujrimīn: those who reject and do wrong. Allah’s wisdom will never treat them the same.
35.why: The disbelievers of Makkah told the believers: “We will be given better than you in the Hereafter.” This ayah was revealed in reply.

36.explain: Mā lakum: what is wrong with you? Kayfa taḥkumūn: how can you make such a false judgement?

37.explain: Do you have a kitāb, a book sent down from Allah, that you tadrusūn, study and recite?

38.explain: …that says you will get whatever you choose (takhayyarūn)? No such book exists.

39.explain: Aymān: firm pledges from Allah to you, lasting until the Day of Resurrection, that you will get whatever you decide for yourselves?

40.explain: Salhum: ask them. Zaʿīm: a guarantor. Which of them will stand surety for this claim? None can.

41.explain: Shurakāʾ: partners who agree with them and back their claim, or witnesses to it. If they have any, let them bring them.

42.explain: Yukshafu ʿan sāq: the shin is uncovered, meaning either the hour of greatest terror, or Allah revealing His Shin as the hadith describes. All are called to prostrate; disbelievers and hypocrites cannot bend.

43.explain: Khāshiʿatan abṣāruhum: eyes lowered in shame. Tarhaquhum dhillah: disgrace covers them. In this world they were called to prostrate, by the call to prayer, while sālimūn, healthy and able, and refused.

44.explain: Fa-dharnī: leave him to Me; don’t let him weigh on your heart. Hādhā al-ḥadīth: the Qurʾan. Sa-nastadrijuhum: We lead them step by step toward punishment, while they think it is blessing.

45.explain: Umlī lahum: I give them respite and extend their time. Kaydī matīn: My plan is firm. Allah gives the wrongdoer time, then seizes him, and he cannot escape.

46.explain: Do you ask them for ajr, a payment, so they are weighed down by maghram, a debt? No: the Prophet ﷺ calls them for their own good and asks nothing.

47.explain: Or do they have al-ghayb, the unseen, and copy from it proof that they are right? They don’t; they are simply stubborn.

48.explain: Li-ḥukmi rabbik: for what your Lord decrees and rules. Ṣāḥib al-ḥūt: Yūnus. Don’t share his impatience with his people. Makẓūm: filled with grief as he called out inside the fish.

49.explain: Niʿmah: a favour, his repentance accepted. Otherwise he would have been thrown from the fish onto al-ʿarāʾ, bare open land, madhmūm, blamed. He was thrown out, but not in blame.

50.explain: Ijtabāhu: his Lord chose and purified him, and made him one of aṣ-ṣāliḥīn, the righteous. The Prophet ﷺ said no one should say, “I am better than Yūnus ibn Mattā.”

51.explain: Layuzliqūnaka bi-abṣārihim: they almost make you slip with their eyes, either through the evil eye, out of envy, or by staring with such hatred it could knock you down, when they hear the Qurʾan.
51.why: Reportedly the disbelievers asked a man famous for striking camels with the evil eye to do the same to the Prophet ﷺ. He tried and failed. Allah protected the Prophet ﷺ and revealed this ayah.

52.explain: Dhikr lil-ʿālamīn: a reminder and admonition for jinn and humankind. A madman could never bring it. It is reported that ayat 51–52 are recited over someone struck by the evil eye.
